name: Utilities
tagline: Critical electricity infrastructure. Safety first, availability second.

org.name: Gridline Energy
org.brief: A regional distributor that keeps roughly 800,000 customers connected. A corporate IT network, a thin IT/OT DMZ and an ADMS/SCADA master that switches substations are separated by policy more than by architecture. A vendor team has remote support access to the control network.

regimes.name: Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018 (Cth)
regimes.note: Responsible entities for critical electricity assets must maintain a critical infrastructure risk management program and report cyber security incidents to the ACSC — within 12 hours when the impact on availability is significant, and 72 hours otherwise.

regimes.name: AESCSF
regimes.note: AEMO’s Australian Energy Sector Cyber Security Framework: a maturity-based self-assessment against the energy sector’s risks.

regimes.name: IEC 62443 / NIST SP 800-82
regimes.note: The usual technical baselines for zones, conduits and ICS security.

assets.name: Corporate Email
assets.desc: Staff email, rostering and procurement traffic.

assets.name: Vendor & Remote Access
assets.desc: VPN and remote-support portal used by staff and OT vendors.

assets.name: Corporate Endpoints
assets.desc: Office laptops, some used by engineers.

assets.name: Corporate Identity (AD)
assets.desc: Active Directory trusted by the DMZ.

assets.name: AMI Head-End & Billing
assets.desc: Smart-meter head-end, meter data and billing.

assets.name: IT/OT DMZ & Historian
assets.desc: Jump hosts and the process historian.

assets.name: ADMS / SCADA Master
assets.desc: The control-room system that sees and switches the network.

assets.name: Substation RTUs & Relays
assets.desc: Field devices that open and close breakers.

systems.name: IT/OT boundary & control network
systems.blurb: Vendors and corporate staff reach the control network through a DMZ. The SCADA master switches substations using DNP3 over the OT network.

scenarios.text: A contractor’s stolen credentials are used from overseas to open a remote-support session that the gateway treats as the vendor’s.
scenarios.why: The attacker is being accepted as someone they are not. Nothing has been altered or exposed yet; the failure is identity assurance for a third party.

scenarios.text: On a flat substation network an attacker alters the setpoint values inside control messages travelling between the master and a relay.
scenarios.why: The content of legitimate commands is modified in transit. The relay would act on altered values; confidentiality and availability are not the issue.

scenarios.text: The DMZ historian holds years of load profiles and network topology and is readable from corporate IT with a default read-only account.
scenarios.why: Sensitive operational data is exposed to people who do not need it. It helps an adversary plan, but no data is changed and no service is degraded.

scenarios.text: A vendor technician’s limited account on the jump host exploits a local misconfiguration to become administrator and pivot towards the OT zone.
scenarios.why: A low-privilege identity gains rights it was never granted. The technician is not impersonating anyone (Spoofing); they escalated within their own account.

scenarios.text: An attacker with write access to the logic project repository quietly changes a protection setting that will be deployed at the next maintenance window.
scenarios.why: Stored data (the logic project) is altered without authority and will later be trusted. It is not disclosure or denial; it is integrity.

scenarios.text: A faulty vendor patch crashes the SCADA master’s polling service and operators lose view and control of the network during a storm.
scenarios.why: The service becomes unavailable to its legitimate users at the worst moment. No attacker needs to have forged, changed or read anything.

scenarios.text: Engineers log in to a shared “engineering” account to push a change. Later no one can show which engineer approved it.
scenarios.why: Individuals can deny actions because the shared identity gives no attributable evidence. The remedy is named accounts and logging, not a stronger password.

scenarios.text: Outage and load data sent to the market interface crosses an unencrypted link and is captured by a third party.
scenarios.why: The contents of the data flow are readable by an eavesdropper. Altering or blocking the flow would be a different threat.

systems.name: Smart meters & customer platform
systems.blurb: Smart meters report interval data to a head-end; meter data feeds billing and a customer portal that holds sensitive account details.

scenarios.text: An attacker uses leaked personal details to impersonate a customer on the phone and redirect account notices to a new email address.
scenarios.why: The attacker poses as a legitimate customer. The portal’s data and availability are unaffected; the weakness is how identity is verified.

scenarios.text: Changing the account number in a portal URL returns another customer’s usage history and street address.
scenarios.why: Customer data is disclosed to someone who is not authorised for it (broken object-level authorisation). Nothing is modified, and the attacker did not escalate their role.

scenarios.text: A compromised mesh node rewrites interval reads in transit so a large consumer’s usage appears lower.
scenarios.why: Data is altered while moving between the meter and head-end. This is integrity, not confidentiality or availability.

scenarios.text: Any customer-support role can trigger the head-end’s mass remote-disconnect function because the capability was never restricted.
scenarios.why: A role can perform a powerful action it should never have been granted. The failure is authorisation design, not identity or logging.

scenarios.text: An insider edits stored meter-read values to avoid a large bill; the original reads are not retained anywhere.
scenarios.why: Stored data is modified without authority. The absence of retained originals makes it worse, but the threat applied to this store is tampering.

scenarios.text: A $40,000 billing adjustment is approved but the system records only the approver’s team name, not the individual.
scenarios.why: There is no attributable evidence of who authorised the action — the defining Repudiation problem.

scenarios.text: A nightly export of customer records, including addresses of customers on life-support equipment, is left in a publicly readable storage bucket.
scenarios.why: Sensitive records stored at rest become readable by the public. The data is unchanged and the service is up, so this is disclosure.

scenarios.text: During a heatwave outage a botnet floods the portal while customers check restoration times, and the site goes down.
scenarios.why: Traffic is used to make the service unavailable to legitimate users when it is needed most.

ttx.name: Blackout Rehearsal
ttx.blurb: An Industroyer-style attack on a distributor, modelled on the documented December 2016 attack on Ukrainian electric power (MITRE C0025). Keep supply, make the SOCI call, and ground your decisions in safety.

injects.title: A quiet Friday evening
injects.text: A corporate engineer opens a “rostering update” spreadsheet. Nothing visibly happens.

injects.title: The mouse moves by itself
injects.text: The control-room operator reports cursor movement on an HMI they are not touching, and a breaker status flickers on the display.

decision.prompt: What does the shift supervisor do?

choices.label: Switch affected feeders to local/manual control, disconnect the HMI network segment, and preserve the workstation state for forensics.
choices.lesson: In OT, keep the lights on first: manual control and isolation come before forensics purity, but preserve what you can.

choices.label: Watch the screen and ask IT to investigate remotely.
choices.lesson: Observing without containing gives the adversary more time and may let them reach protection systems.

choices.label: Reboot the HMI to clear the problem.
choices.lesson: A reboot destroys evidence and may drop operators’ view of the grid while the adversary still holds the master.

injects.title: Is this reportable under SOCI?
injects.text: The compliance lead asks whether this is a notifiable cyber security incident and how fast.

choices.label: Treat it as a critical cyber security incident: report to the ACSC within 12 hours of becoming aware because availability is significantly impacted, and follow with the written report.
choices.lesson: SOCI distinguishes incidents with a significant impact on availability (12 hours) from other relevant impacts (72 hours). When in doubt, report early.

choices.label: Wait for the forensic report to decide whether it is significant.
choices.lesson: The clock starts when you become aware, not when forensics finishes.

choices.label: Do not report: supply has not actually been lost.
choices.lesson: Reportability turns on impact and the incident’s nature, not on whether the outage was finally prevented.

injects.title: AEMO is on the line
injects.text: AEMO’s operations team asks whether you can shed load manually and hold the network stable while the incident is contained.

choices.label: Coordinate with AEMO: confirm manual switching capability, keep the compromised master isolated, and agree a communications cadence.
choices.lesson: Sector coordination is a control: AEMO and state agencies need accurate capability and constraint information.

choices.label: Promise normal service and defer details until morning.
choices.lesson: Overpromising during an incident erodes trust and complicates system operation.

choices.label: Reconnect the master to confirm everything is fine.
choices.lesson: Reconnecting a suspected-compromised master to the live network invites worse.

injects.title: The vendor wants to push firmware
injects.text: The relay vendor offers an emergency firmware update delivered remotely to all substations “to close the hole”.

choices.label: Decline remote push. Obtain the signed firmware, verify it offline, and deploy it under supervision in a planned, staged way.
choices.lesson: During an incident, a vendor’s remote update channel is itself an attack path. Verify and stage updates.

choices.label: Accept immediately; speed matters.
choices.lesson: An unverified remote push to every substation risks a fleet-wide fault.

choices.label: Defer all updates indefinitely.
choices.lesson: Never patching leaves the original weakness in place.

injects.title: “Hackers black out suburb?”
injects.text: A news site is asking whether a cyber attack caused tonight’s outage.

choices.label: Confirm you are investigating a possible cyber incident, that supply is being restored manually, and that you are working with government agencies; commit to updates.
choices.lesson: Accurate, measured disclosure supports public safety and avoids speculation.

choices.label: Deny any cyber link.
choices.lesson: A denial that is later reversed is costlier than a holding statement.

choices.label: No comment.
choices.lesson: Silence leaves customers without safety information.

objectives.text: Keep the SCADA master and substation relays under your control

govern.spoofing.name: Remote Access & Vendor Policy
govern.spoofing.flavour: No vendor session without a ticket and a name
govern.spoofing.desc: Policy that governs who may reach the control network, how, when and under whose supervision: named vendor accounts, approved windows, MFA and session recording.

govern.dos.name: CIRMP & Impact Tolerance
govern.dos.flavour: How long can a feeder stay dark?
govern.dos.desc: A risk management program that sets maximum tolerable outage for critical functions and funds the controls to meet it. The foundation of SOCI compliance.

identify.dos.name: Critical Asset & Dependency Register
identify.dos.flavour: Every feeder, relay and the radio link they share
identify.dos.desc: Inventory of critical electricity assets and what each depends on — communications, power, vendors, people — so a single dependency failure is understood before it happens.

identify.disclosure.name: Purdue Network & Data-Flow Map
identify.disclosure.flavour: If it is not on the diagram, it is not secured
identify.disclosure.desc: Current diagrams of zones, conduits and data flows across IT, DMZ and OT, including the vendor paths nobody remembers authorising.

protect.spoofing.name: Operator & Vendor MFA
protect.spoofing.flavour: Hardware tokens at the HMI door
protect.spoofing.desc: Strong, preferably hardware-bound multi-factor authentication for operators, engineers and vendors, enforced at the remote-access gateway and again before the control zone.

protect.tampering.name: Signed Firmware & Logic Integrity
protect.tampering.flavour: Only code the utility approved reaches a relay
protect.tampering.desc: Signed firmware and controller logic, verified at load, with baselines for protection settings. Counters tampering with logic and configuration.

protect.elevation.name: Zone-Based Least Privilege
protect.elevation.desc: Role-based access per IEC 62443 zone and conduit: engineers reach what they maintain, vendors reach nothing standing, and privilege in IT never implies privilege in OT.

detect.tampering.name: Passive OT Network Monitoring
detect.tampering.desc: Passive monitoring of OT traffic and asset behaviour that never sends probes into fragile devices, flagging new devices, new commands and changed logic.

respond.tampering.name: Segment Isolation & Manual Fallback
respond.tampering.flavour: Cut the link; switch it by hand
respond.tampering.desc: Pre-agreed ability to sever the IT/OT conduit and run substations under local or manual control while the investigation proceeds. Safety and supply continuity outrank forensics purity.

respond.disclosure.name: SOCI Incident Reporting Playbook
respond.disclosure.flavour: The 12-hour clock starts when you become aware
respond.disclosure.desc: Decision tree and drafts for reporting a cyber security incident to the ACSC under SOCI — including who decides if the impact is significant — alongside notifications to AEMO and the state regulator.

recover.dos.name: Black-Start & Offline Control Backups
recover.dos.flavour: Rebuild the control room from tape
recover.dos.desc: Offline backups of SCADA/ADMS configurations and controller logic, with tested procedures to restore the control system and perform a black start when everything else is down.

cards.name: Unidirectional Gateway
cards.desc: A hardware data diode lets telemetry flow out of the control zone but nothing flow in. Spread into or out of this asset costs +1 and has −1 power.
cards.lesson: Hardware-enforced one-way flow removes whole classes of inbound attack from a zone, at the price of flexibility.

cards.name: Manual Operations Fallback
cards.desc: Operators switch to local and manual control while IT is isolated. Heals the asset, restores its controls and isolates it.
cards.lesson: Rehearsed manual operation is the ultimate availability control for the grid. Practise it before you need it.

cards.name: Passive OT Monitor
cards.desc: Listens to OT traffic without probing devices: reveals up to 2 footholds per round (stealth ≤ 4) on this asset.
cards.lesson: Active scanning can crash fragile controllers. Passive monitoring is the safe default in OT.

cards.name: Authenticated Control Commands
cards.desc: Control messages are authenticated end to end. Counters Manipulation of Control.
cards.lesson: Industrial protocols were designed for trust. Authenticating commands closes the gap between “reachable” and “allowed to operate”.

relics.name: CIRMP Uplift Programme
relics.lesson: A funded, board-owned risk management program is what turns standards into operating capability.
